subtype: Approach: rechecks the backward chain against real progress and reschedules [Revision]
passage: At month three of the plan, Salma's checkpoint, finishing the first reading block, had slipped by two weeks, because quarter-end at the firm swallowed her evenings. The finance qualification exam sat in November. Salma, a young analyst, pushed her chair back on a noisy Saturday, with a wedding band playing next door, and pulled the sheet toward her. Instead of squeezing the old dates, she started from the exam again: last mock in mid-October, so practice must end by then, so the second reading block must finish by late August. Then she looked at the optional data certificate she had added in a keen moment. It no longer fit. She struck it out and sent Mahima, her study partner, the new dates that night.

qa.q: Why had Salma's month-three checkpoint slipped?
qa.a: It had slipped because quarter-end at the firm swallowed her evenings.

qa.q: What was Salma probably feeling as she looked at the slipped checkpoint?
qa.a: Salma was probably worried and pressed for time, but she chose to redo the dates from the exam instead of panicking.

qa.q: What other approach could help Salma keep the new dates?
qa.a: Salma could ask her manager for a few study days close to the exam, since a fixed block of free time protects the last stretch of the plan.

qa.q: How might Mahima see the new dates?
qa.a: Mahima would probably feel glad to have clear dates and see that Salma is facing the slip honestly, though maybe a little worried about the tighter schedule.

grounding: Shows an analyst noticing a slipping checkpoint, re-deriving later milestones from the exam date and dropping an optional certificate.
